sections.body_en:
It is a positive Torah commandment to lend money to a person who needs it, as it is said (Shemot 22:24): "If you lend money to My people." Now, wherever the Torah says 'if', the meaning is something optional – if you wish, you lend, and if you do not wish, you do not lend. But here our Sages said in the Mekhilta that this is one of the three places where the Torah used the word 'if' even though the intention is a mitzva that one is obligated to fulfil. And the truth is that the word 'if' is not directed at the mitzva, but refers to the end of the verse: if you lend and the borrower does not have money to repay, you shall not be to him as a creditor (Ahavat Ḥesed 1, note 2). The conclusion, then, is that just as there is a mitzva to put on tefillin and to read the Shema, so there is a positive mitzva to lend money to a person who needs it (SA ḤM 97:1).

And the Sages said in tractate Shabbat (63a) that this mitzva is greater than the mitzva of tzedaka. And so the Rambam wrote in Sefer Ha-Mitzvot (197): that God commanded us to lend to the poor person in order to ease his poverty and give him relief, and this is a mitzva stronger and more obligatory than all the mitzvot of tzedaka; for one whose poverty has already been revealed in public and who stretches out his hand for charity – his distress and shame are not like the distress of the poor person who hides, who wants to be helped before his poverty is revealed in public and he is humiliated. Therefore the mitzva of lending comes first and is preferable to the mitzva of tzedaka, in that it has extra consideration for the suffering of the other.

And there is another advantage of the mitzva of lending over the ordinary mitzva of tzedaka: the mitzva of lending applies both to the poor and to the rich, whereas tzedaka is only for the poor (Sukka 49b). That is, the kindness expressed in the mitzva of lending is more general and comprehensive, and touches on all the relationships between a person and his fellow, whereas tzedaka is an expression of kindness only towards a certain kind of people. And although it is said in the verse, "If you lend money to My people, to the poor person with you," the meaning is not that there is no mitzva to lend to a rich person; rather, the meaning is that if a rich person and a poor person came to borrow, one should give precedence to the poor person over the rich, because his need for the loan is a greater need (Bava Metzia 71a; SA ḤM 97:1).

And had the Torah not said that one should give precedence to the poor person, most people would prefer to lend to the rich, because there is more security that the rich will be able to return the money, and even in the future repay kindness with kindness, which is not so with the poor person, who has no possibility of doing so. Therefore the Torah needed to emphasise "to the poor person with you" – to give the poor person precedence over the rich (Ahavat Ḥesed 1:1).

The most complicated question in the mitzva of lending is how much money a person must lend his fellow and for how long. Of course, if we are speaking about a very wealthy person, who has no problem at all lending, it is fitting that he grant loans according to need: if he is asked for a large loan, he should give a large loan, and if he is asked for a long-term loan, he should give it for a long term.

But the needs of Your people are many, and a pit is not filled from its own earth, and the wealthy who could supply all the needs of the people have not yet been found. So when a friend or relative comes to us asking for a loan, and we do not have the possibility of helping him according to his need, the question arises: how much money must we lend, or to what extent must a person economise in his expenses in order to help his friends? Must he, for example, stop savings and investment plans in order to give that money as a loan, or is it a mitzva to stop buying dairy delicacies, or to give up a holiday in a hotel?

First it must be said that it is clear that one cannot set clear measures in this halakha, since there are great differences between one person and another, both in income and in expenses, and consequently it is not possible to set measures in this. Nor can one learn anything from the law of tzedaka. For about tzedaka the Sages said that a person is forbidden to give more than a fifth of his property to tzedaka, lest he become poor and need other people (Ketubot 50a). But a loan is not like tzedaka, for in tzedaka the money does not return, whereas in a loan a person is going to receive his money back, and therefore certainly one can give more than a fifth. And on the other hand, it is not possible to say that he must give all his free money as a loan, for it is possible that in the near future some especially good business opportunity will come his way and he will need the money. And further, if he does not give his money as a loan, he could invest it and derive profits from it. And there is also a certain risk that the money will not be returned. Therefore it is not possible to say that he must give all his money as a loan. And conversely, certainly one cannot evade the mitzva of lending on the pretext that we need all the money in order to keep it circulating and derive profits from it, for if so, what will become of the mitzva of lending?!

Nor is it possible to determine which are unnecessary expenses that it is right to cut in order that a person have money to give his fellow as a loan, and which are not luxuries, because the joy of life depends on them. And the matter changes from person to person.

Since it is impossible to set fixed measures in this, the principle must be emphasised: each person must strive to help his friends as much as possible, without harming his basic needs. And in order that the decision whether he can lend or not be correct, it is very important to learn about the great value of the mitzva of lending, and likewise about the general value of gemilut ḥesed, and from that one can weigh correctly how much money to lend.

Although the Sages said (Makkot 3b) that an unspecified loan is for thirty days, certainly they do not mean to say that there is no mitzva to lend for more than thirty days; rather, the meaning is that if they did not agree between them on the date of repayment, the loan must be repaid after thirty days, for that is the length of an unspecified loan. But this law is not connected to the mitzva of lending itself, and everything depends on one's means. Therefore, one who was approached with a request for a long-term loan, if he has the possibility, is commanded to lend for a long term. And likewise, if he has the possibility of giving a loan only for a few days, it is clear that he is not commanded to give the loan for longer than he is able (Ahavat Ḥesed 1:6).

How many times should he lend to the same person? The Ḥafetz Ḥayim wrote (Ahavat Ḥesed 1:7) that since the mitzva of lending belongs to the system of mitzvot included in gemilut ḥasadim, its law consequently is that it has no fixed measure. And just as in all the mitzvot of gemilut ḥasadim, every time a new need arises there is a mitzva to help, so too is the law regarding a loan. And just as one may not say to a sick person who needs help, "Sorry, since I already helped you once today, I have fulfilled my obligation, and from now on manage by yourself," so too one should not refrain from lending to one person several times. And even if a person came to his fellow and asked him for a loan, and a short time after repaying the loan asked for another loan, even up to a hundred times – each and every time, if he has the ability to lend, he should lend with joy and affection. And he should think that every time he lends he fulfils a mitzva, and if so, why should he mind lending again and again? If he were a shopkeeper, and a person knocked on the doors of his shop again and again in order to buy the same goods, would he be angry with him and claim to him, "But you already bought once today, why are you coming twice?!" Certainly not, for on each and every purchase he profits. So too must a person who grants a loan think: every time he lends he fulfils a mitzva, and therefore he is the great gainer from having merited to lend to his fellow.

sections.title_en: 4. Lending at Interest and the Heter Iska
sections.body_en:
There are two forms of loans: one excellent and without equal, and the other bad. The good loan is the loan whose main purpose is to do kindness with the other and to help him. And the bad loan is the loan at interest, whose whole purpose is selfish. One can do almost the same act – lend money to a friend – but when one lends without interest the purpose is to help, and one fulfils a mitzva; and when one lends at interest, the purpose is to exploit the other's distress and become rich, and this is a severe sin. The Shulḥan Arukh wrote (YD 160:2): "Whoever gives a loan at interest – his property collapses, and it is as though he denied the Exodus from Egypt and the God of Israel." For we have already left Egypt, and through that it became known to us that materialism is not the main thing. Hashem, may He be blessed, has already been revealed to us and taught us ways of life and kindness. And how is it possible that a Jew would exploit the hard situation of his fellow, and his desperate need for money, in order to become rich? It can only be that he has deteriorated into denial of the God of Israel and of the Exodus from Egypt. Therefore the punishment of the one who lends at interest is also great, that his property collapses, and the Sages compared him to a snake.

And not only the one who lends at interest transgresses a prohibition, but also the borrower and the witnesses and the guarantors, and everyone who takes part in this forbidden loan transgresses a Torah prohibition.

But there is the well-known "heter iska", whose essence is that this is not a loan at all but a business of partners: one gives money and the other gives work, and afterwards they divide the profits. For example, one has money for investment and the other has a factory; the owner of the money invests the money in the factory, thereby the factory owner can increase production, and afterwards they will share the profits. And in order not to get entangled in accounting difficulties, they fix from the outset the share of the one who gave the money – that he will earn such-and-such a percentage every year – while the rest of the profits the worker will receive. And indeed the logic of the "heter iska" is clear: there is no reason for the owner of the money to take cash out of his pocket and finance the worker or the factory; rather, there is a partnership here from which both sides need to profit.

But one must be very careful that, heaven forbid, the "heter iska" not cancel and cause us to forget the important mitzva of giving a loan to the needy. For the whole "heter iska" is based on the worker not being in distress, and the aim of both of them is to profit and become rich, and therefore the owner of the money has the right to be a partner in the profits. But when we are speaking of a person in distress, who has nothing to live on, or who has no possibility of buying an apartment, and the like, we are certainly obligated to strive to help him as far as we are able with a loan without interest.

sections.title_en: 5. Does One Who Is in Overdraft Transgress the Prohibition of Interest?
sections.body_en:
Question: Is a person permitted to be in the minus (overdraft) in his bank account, and to pay interest on it under a "heter iska"?

Answer: In the view of most poskim, a person is forbidden to make an overdraft withdrawal from the bank not for business purposes. And although the bank has a "heter iska" on all its transactions, this does not help for an overdraft for the purpose of ongoing living costs, because the basis of the permission rests on the money being invested in transactions for the purpose of profit, and therefore this is not a loan but a business transaction. But if the money is intended for buying food and clothes and other needs, this is an ordinary loan, not intended for investments, and consequently the percentages added to the principal are interest forbidden by Torah law. And although some permit this in a time of pressing need, nevertheless the view of most poskim is that it is forbidden by Torah law for a person to be in the minus at the bank in order to finance his purchases.

However, one who has a savings plan or an apartment, and for a certain period found himself in financial distress, and in order to finance his ongoing needs he has two options before him – either to break the savings plan or sell the apartment, or to withdraw sums of money from the bank and afterwards pay interest on them – in a time of pressing need he is permitted to enter the minus (overdraft) and afterwards pay interest on it. This is because this withdrawal can be considered a business need, for if he has to sell the apartment or break the savings plan, he will suffer a financial loss; and therefore it is more worthwhile for him to be in the minus and pay a certain interest on it, and thereby save himself the loss involved in breaking the savings plan or selling the apartment.

But this permission too may be used only for a limited time. For in the case of a permanent deficit, one cannot say that it is better for him not to break a savings plan or not to sell the apartment, since the interest he receives for his savings, or the gain he receives from keeping his apartment, is smaller than the interest he pays over a long period for an overdraft.[1]

notes_en.en: The Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav wrote (Laws of Interest 42) that it is forbidden to make a "heter iska" for ongoing expenses, but only for a business need. And so wrote many poskim. Indeed, some permit it when it is worth more to him to pay the interest than to live in great hardship, and then this too is considered a business transaction. And so it is implied by the words of Responsa Sho'el U-meshiv, Mahadura Kamma 3:160 and Telita'ah 1:137, and Maharsham 2:216. But according to most poskim the matter is forbidden, and so wrote Peraḥ Shoshan YD rule 6, Har Ha-Karmel ḤM 25, Ḥayim Be-Yad 41, Imrei Yosher 108, Teshuvat Shai 88, Maharshag YD 4, 37, and many others. But if he enters the minus in order to avoid a greater loss from breaking a savings plan, one may be lenient, and so many Aḥaronim ruled. See the book Torat Ha-Ribit 16:15, and Ribit Le-Or Ha-Halakha 23:14 and 24:13.

sections.title_en: 6. Must a Banker or a Grocer Lend?
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of lending is a general mitzva incumbent on every Jew, man and woman alike, rich and poor alike: whenever a Jew whose financial situation is worse than his own comes to him, if he has free money in his possession, he is commanded to lend it to his fellow. And it is written in the book Ahavat Ḥesed (part 1, 2:3) that even a person whose business is lending under a "heter iska", and in this way he earns a certain percentage on his money every year and lives from this – even such a person is not exempt from the mitzva of lending, and he must calculate how much money he can lend to the needy without interest.

And regarding a grocer, Ahavat Ḥesed wrote (part 1, 2:5) that he is not obligated by the mitzva of lending to sell to his customers on credit. That is, certainly in his private capacity he must fulfil the mitzva of lending, but in the shop he is not obligated to sell on credit. And even if he agreed that they pay him every two weeks, he is not obligated to agree to extend credit for a longer time. And the reason is that a sale is not a loan, and consequently a seller who extends credit to his customers does not fulfil the mitzva of lending. And if you say: although there is no mitzva of lending here, nevertheless there is in extending credit an element of kindness towards the customers – the answer to this is that if many people ask the seller to do kindness with them, the seller will not be able to continue the business and buy new goods and develop his shop; therefore he has no mitzva to sell on credit beyond what is customary. In other words, kindness should not disrupt commercial life. Business must be conducted honestly, in a way that it will be worthwhile for everyone to work and to profit. And above this comes kindness, in order to help those who did not manage to get by.

Therefore, in exceptional cases, if a poor person who has nothing to keep himself alive turns to the grocer, certainly the grocer is commanded to help him. And if he is able to sell a little merchandise on credit, or even to give it to him as a gift, he is commanded to do so. For even if there is no mitzva of lending here, nevertheless there is a mitzva of tzedaka here, as it is said (Vayikra 25:35): "And if your brother becomes poor and his hand falters with you, you shall uphold him."

sections.title_en: 7. A Loan Must Not Be Used for Luxuries
sections.body_en:
An important halakha is brought in the Shulḥan Arukh (ḤM 93:4): "The borrower is forbidden to take a loan and spend it needlessly and lose it, until the lender finds nothing from which to collect his debt. And if he does so – he is called wicked. And when the lender knows that the borrower has this trait, it is better not to lend to him than to lend to him and have to press him afterwards and transgress each time 'you shall not be to him as a creditor.'"

We learn an important principle in this se'if: the borrower is forbidden to take a loan and spend it needlessly on all kinds of luxuries, lest afterwards he be unable to repay it. And so the author of Me'irat Einayim explained (note 5) that the intention of the Shulḥan Arukh is that anything which is not a great need for a person is considered needless, and one who uses a loan needlessly is considered as though he loses it. And the Shulḥan Arukh added a sharp remark: that the borrower who squanders the money of the loan on unimportant things is called wicked. The reason for this is that in every loan there is a certain risk that the borrower will not be able to return the money, and we are commanded by the Torah to enter into this risk in order to help a friend stand on his feet and survive; but the Torah did not command us to take a risk in order to help a friend buy luxuries or to finance his unnecessary trips and travels.

And even if the borrower is certain that he will be able to repay the debt in the end, even then he is forbidden to use the loan for luxuries without explicit permission from the lender; for as stated, a loan is generally given in order to buy an apartment or in order to survive and get through a few difficult months, but not in order to squander it on luxuries.

And what is considered a luxury and what is not a luxury depends on the period and on the society to which the lender and borrower belong. For example, one who wants to take a loan from his friend or from a gemaḥ in order to buy a new car certainly must, according to halakha, inform the lender of this explicitly, and ask him for the loan in order to buy a new car. Whereas one who asks for a loan for the purpose of buying a simple refrigerator need not ask explicit permission from the lender to use the loan for this purpose, because a refrigerator is not considered a luxury today.

sections.title_en: 8. Lending to Trustworthy People and in a Secure Manner
sections.body_en:
It happens that a person wants to be good and do kindness with his fellow and lend him money, but matters become complicated and the borrower denies the loan and refuses to return it. And sometimes the borrower does not deny the loan, but claims that he has no money to return, and at the same time makes no effort at all to work and earn money in order to repay his debt; and so, after the lender chases after him, he agrees from time to time to return to him a certain part of the loan. And in the end only harm comes from that loan: the lender loses money and time, and in addition he is caused disappointment with acts of kindness, while the borrower is considered wicked, as it is said (Tehillim 37:21): "The wicked borrows and does not repay." In order not to come to this, the Shulḥan Arukh ruled (ḤM 97:4) that one should not lend money to a person of bad traits, a squanderer or irresponsible, about whom there is a reasonable concern that he will not repay his debt.

And even when one lends to an upright person, it happens that unintentionally he forgets the loan, and afterwards, when the lender comes to claim from him, he denies the loan. In order to prevent such a situation, halakha ruled (SA 70:1) that it is forbidden to lend without witnesses, lest the borrower forget the loan and not pay, and transgress robbery. And if there are no witnesses, or when one wants to keep the matter of the loan secret, there are two more options: either to lend with a document, so that everything is written and recorded – what the sum of the loan is and when it must be returned – or to lend against a pledge, for certainly in such a case the borrower will not forget the loan, and even if he forgets, the pledge will remind him. And the Shulḥan Arukh adds that even if the loan is intended for a Torah scholar, who certainly should not be suspected of deliberately denying the loan and refusing to pay, nevertheless one must lend with witnesses or a document or against a pledge. The reason is that a Torah scholar, because of his preoccupation and immersion in study, is liable to forget the loan. And in order not to come to such an unpleasant case, it is a mitzva to lend only with a document or witnesses or a pledge.

And if the lender does not do so, the Shulḥan Arukh wrote that he transgresses "Before a blind person you shall not put a stumbling block" (Vayikra 19:14), and brings a curse on himself, for people will curse him and say: here is a man who claims from his fellow what he does not owe him.

And if a person comes and asks: "Even when I lend my friend a small sum for a bus fare, for example, must I take the trouble to bring witnesses or write a document? It is impossible to live in such a complicated way!" The answer to this is that two options stand before the lender: either to write a document as written in the Shulḥan Arukh, or to decide in his heart that if the borrower forgets the loan, he forgoes it to him wholeheartedly, and the loan will become a gift. And then, even if the borrower truly forgets the loan, he will not transgress the prohibition of robbery. And certainly the lender and borrower will not quarrel between themselves, since the lender has already agreed in his heart to forgive. And the same law applies to a woman who lends her friend cheese and the like: either they record the loan, or the giver agrees in her mind that if the neighbour forgets the loan, she forgives her wholeheartedly.

sections.title_en: 9. One Should Not Be Afraid to Lend
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, when the one asking for the loan is known as a person who is not trustworthy, and it is likely that he will not repay the debt, there is no mitzva to lend to him. And it is even better not to lend to him, since from this loan love and peace will not grow, but quarrel and strife. And even if that person asking for the loan is poor and truly needs money, one should not give him a loan, because of "Before a blind person you shall not put a stumbling block". But one should try to help him under the law of tzedaka. And generally, when it comes to tzedaka, the sums are lower, since the money is not going to return.

However, one must beware of excessive caution, and not suspect people too much that they will not return the debt. Many times the fear of lending does not stem from genuine caution, but from an excessive love of money. In the eyes of the miser, no person will guard his money as he truly wants it to be guarded. But the truth is that most people are trustworthy and return their debt; and therefore only when it is known that a certain person is not like this should one not lend to him.

The Ḥafetz Ḥayim, in his book Ahavat Ḥesed, explains at length the great merit of the mitzva of lending, and he expands with words of musar, and says that a person from whom a loan is requested should not think that he has received a punishment and been sentenced to help his fellow; on the contrary, a great privilege has fallen to his lot, to help his fellow. And if a person says, "Since several times already I lent friends money and they did not return it, I do not want to continue lending any more," we will answer him: a shopkeeper from whom many buy on credit – and of course from time to time there are those who do not pay – will he because of this stop the business and close his shop? Certainly not; this is the order of the world, in every good business there are also losses from time to time. Exactly the same thinking must apply also regarding lending: it is a wonderful privilege to help a friend, and there is hardly anything more exalted and noble than this act. If so, because of a few isolated cases of people who did not return the loan, shall we lose this successful business of the mitzva of lending?!

This is only one of the beautiful parables brought in the book Ahavat Ḥesed about the mitzva of lending and kindness.

sections.title_en: 10. Which Is Preferable, Several Small Loans or One Large One?
sections.body_en:
Sometimes a person faces the question of what to do in a case where two options stand before him: to give several small loans to several people, or to give one large loan to one person. For example, a person who has the possibility of lending ten thousand shekels, and eleven people came before him: ten of them ask for a thousand shekels each, and one asks for the whole ten thousand shekels. Is it preferable to give one large loan to one person, or ten small loans to ten people?

An answer to this is brought in the book Ahavat Ḥesed (1:14), and this is its essence: in principle it is better to lend small sums to several people than to lend a large sum to one person. For with each and every loan one fulfils a mitzva, and increases peace and friendship between a person and his fellow. And so the Rambam wrote that a person who wishes to give a certain sum to tzedaka – it is preferable that he divide it and give it on many occasions, because every time he gives tzedaka his soul is refined and rises to the heights of kindness; and this is what the Sages said (Avot 3:15): "Everything is according to the abundance of the deed."

And all this is on condition that all those asking for a loan are equal in their order of precedence. But if the person asking for the large loan is in such a situation that without the loan he may collapse financially and go bankrupt, and with the help of the loan he will be able to continue his business and restore it, while the other people do not need the loan in order to save their future, then it is preferable to lend one large loan in order to save that person from bankruptcy. And this is because in this loan one fulfils, in addition to the ordinary mitzva of lending, the Torah's mitzva (Vayikra 25:35): "And if your brother becomes poor and his hand falters with you, you shall uphold him." And the Rambam already mentioned that the highest of the levels of tzedaka is to help a person who is about to go bankrupt, in such a way that he will be able to continue and sustain himself afterwards by his own strength. Therefore, whenever it is possible to put a person back on his feet, he comes before all the others.

The difficult problem is that even after we have decided to allocate part of our money to gemilut ḥasadim by lending money, even then the question arises of whom to help first. For the needs of the people are many, and certainly we will not be able to give a loan to everyone who asks, and therefore an order of priorities must be set.

And indeed a whole sugya in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 71a) deals with the order of precedence in the mitzva of lending, and from it the order of precedence for all the mitzvot of kindness in the Torah was learned. The source of the teaching is from the verse (Shemot 22:24): "If you lend money to My people, to the poor person with you." Several principles can be learned from this verse. First, the poor of Israel and the poor of the gentiles – the poor of Israel come first, as it is said: "lend money to My people" – first one must help and lend to the members of your people, and only afterwards to members of other peoples. And the Torah adds and says, "to the poor person with you," to teach us that if a poor person and a rich person came before us, we must give precedence and lend to the poor person, and only if money remains may one lend to the rich. And the Gemara further infers from the word "with you" that the nearer always comes first; therefore, a poor person of your own town and a poor person of another town – it is a mitzva to give precedence to the poor person from the same town. And even if two residents of the same town came, one from your neighbourhood and the other from another neighbourhood, it is a mitzva to give precedence to the one from your neighbourhood, who is more "with you". And even if both are from the same neighbourhood, but one of them is a near neighbour and the other lives some distance away, it is a mitzva to give precedence to the near neighbour (YD 251:3; Ahavat Ḥesed part 1, 6:2).

And not only regarding residence is the principle that the nearer comes first, but also regarding family: a close relative comes before a distant one. Therefore parents come before brothers, and brothers before uncles, and uncles before cousins, and so on (YD there; Ahavat Ḥesed part 1, 6:4).

These laws of precedence do not concern only the mitzva of lending, but also all the other laws of gemilut ḥasadim. For example, when there are two sick people who need our help, and we are not able to help both of them, it is a mitzva to give precedence to the sick person who is a relative or a neighbour.

And the reason for all this is clear. It is indeed true that each person must desire the good of all human beings in the world, and not only the good of his brothers and neighbours. But when one begins to repair and help, one must do so in order. For if there is no order, a situation may arise in which there will be some popular poor person whom everyone wants to help, and beside him another poor person to whom nobody pays attention. One will publicise his problem on the radio and everyone will run to help him, while the poor wretch who was ashamed will remain alone without help. Therefore the Torah said that each person should take an interest in the situation of his neighbours and relatives, for those he knows well, and if they need help, he will know about it and be able to extend a hand to them. And if each one of us, wherever he is, pays attention to his neighbours and relatives, we can be sure that all the poor are taken care of, and no person is left without help. For there is hardly a person without relatives. And even if his relatives are few and poor, nevertheless he has neighbours, and they must know his situation and help him.

And one who has merited that the situation of his neighbours and relatives is good is of course not exempt from the mitzva of lending and kindness; rather, his role is to help those further away, the people of his town, the people of his nation. And when all the members of our nation are settled financially, we will continue and do kindness with the whole world. And so, stage after stage, the world will be repaired in the light of our Torah of kindness.

sections.title_en: 12. Giving Precedence to a Jew over a Gentile
sections.body_en:
The Torah taught a special teaching that one should give precedence to a loan to a Jew over a loan to a gentile, as it is said: "If you lend money to My people," to teach that a Jew comes before a gentile (Bava Metzia 71a). And seemingly one could have learned this from the basic principle that the nearer always comes first, as it is said: "to the poor person with you," and it is clear that every Jew is more in the category of "with you" than a member of another nation.

But there is an additional novelty here, for it is permitted to lend to a gentile at interest, and in the view of the Rambam it is even a mitzva to lend to him at interest. If so, the Torah comes and tells us that even though when we lend to the gentile we will earn the interest, whereas when we lend to the Jew we will not receive interest, nevertheless it is a mitzva to give precedence and lend to the Jew, even though we will not earn interest from his loan.

And the same law applies to everything: if a Jew wants to sell something, and a Jew and a gentile come before him, even if the gentile offers a higher sum, it is a mitzva to sell to the Jew and not to the gentile. For it is said (Vayikra 25:14): "And if you sell something to your fellow or buy from the hand of your fellow," and the Sages learned in the Sifra: if you come to sell, give precedence to selling to your fellow Jew; and likewise, if you come to buy, buy from the hand of your fellow Jew. That is, whether in buying or in selling, one should give precedence to a Jew over a gentile. And even if the gentile sells cheaply or is ready to pay a higher price, even then one must give precedence to the Jew over the foreigner (Ahavat Ḥesed part 1, 5:7).

And the same law applies to employing a worker: if there is the possibility of hiring a Jew and a gentile, it is a mitzva to give precedence to the Jew, even if his wage is higher. But if the difference between the Jew and the gentile is very great, in certain cases one may be lenient and prefer the gentile to the Jew. And in every case one must judge the matter on its merits according to the special circumstances, and when there is doubt one should ask a sage (and see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land", chapter 8, on Hebrew labour).

sections.title_en: 13. Summary of the Laws of Precedence in Israel
sections.body_en:
There are three principles in the laws of precedence for the mitzvot of kindness in Israel, and we will list the principles in order of importance. The first principle is that the one in greater need comes before the one in lesser need, and therefore a poor person comes before a rich one. The second principle, that a relative comes before one who is not related. And the third, that a neighbour comes before one who is not a neighbour, and a resident of one's town before a resident of another town. That is, the order of priorities is determined according to three different principles: a) according to the level of need; b) family closeness; c) closeness of place. And it is very important to pay attention to the order of the principles, for in a case where there is a clash between one principle and another, one should prefer the first principle over the second, and the second over the third.

Let us mention some examples. If, for example, a person has a thousand shekels, and two people came before him and asked to borrow it, one of them a relative who lives in another town, and the other a neighbour who is not a relative – that is, there is a clash here between the second principle, according to which one should give precedence to the relative, and the third principle, according to which one should give precedence to the neighbour – since the second principle comes before the third, one should give precedence to the relative over the neighbour. And the reason for this is that family closeness is stronger than neighbourliness; and since the Torah said 'with you', the relative is more 'with you' than the neighbour, and therefore he should be given precedence.[2]

And if a clash arises between the first principle and the second or third, the first principle comes first. For the most important thing of all is to help the needy, and the one in greater need comes before the one in lesser need. For example, if two people come with a request for a loan, one of them a poor stranger who is neither a relative nor a neighbour, while the second is not poor but is both a relative and a neighbour – again there is a clash between the principles, for according to the first principle one should give precedence to the poor person, whereas according to the second and third one should give precedence to the relative neighbour. And since the first principle comes first, one should lend first to the poor person, and only afterwards, if money remains, is it a mitzva to lend it to the relative neighbour (Ahavat Ḥesed part 1, 6:1).

And likewise, if two poor people stand before us, one needing a loan in order to buy food and the second in order to buy clothing, one must give precedence to the one who needs food, since he is more needy and hard-pressed (Ahavat Ḥesed part 1, 6:1).

notes_en.en:
Indeed, there are times when there is a friend who is as close as a brother, and then there is room to give him precedence over relatives, for their close friendship makes him more 'with you' than his relatives. But one must weigh the matter well, for sometimes a friend is very close for a number of years, yet in the long term family closeness is deeper, and the long-term consideration is more important.
And likewise, sometimes a person may decide that he prefers to lend to his relatives, even though they are less poor than others. For since there is no defined obligation of how much he must lend, he is permitted to prefer his relatives. All that we have learned is that if a person has no clear position and asks what the Torah's guidance is, then the guidance is to give precedence to the poorer one. And likewise regarding giving tzedaka: if for various reasons he prefers to help his relatives – for example, because by doing so he will prevent rifts in the family, or because by doing so he will bring them closer to Torah and mitzvot – since there is no obligation to give such-and-such an amount to the needier poor person, he is permitted to give precedence to his relatives.

sections.body_en:
Since the mitzva of lending to the needy without interest is so important and central, it is good for a person to set aside a fixed sum every month into a special account, and the money that accumulates in the account will be designated for loans to the needy. And so, when his relatives or neighbours or acquaintances ask him for a loan, the money will be ready at hand and he will be able to help them by giving the loan. And incidentally, even if he himself at some time needs a loan, he may take from that account, on condition that he returns it all; for otherwise it turns out that he used for his private needs money that was designated for a mitzva.

And many prefer to organise together as a group and set up a gemaḥ fund. Gemaḥ is the acronym of gemilut ḥesed. That is, the purpose of these funds is to help others, each fund according to the rules its founders set. There are gemaḥ funds designated to help poor grooms, there are those designated for the benefit of orphans and widows, and there are those to help the sick and the like. And there are funds that have not defined a particular purpose for themselves, but give a loan to every needy person whoever he may be. Each group is entitled to set for itself the purpose of the gemaḥ according to what seems to it the most important thing at this time.

The Ḥafetz Ḥayim, in his book Ahavat Ḥesed (part 2, chapter 16), devoted a whole chapter to explaining the great obligation that there be in every town a permanent gemaḥ for the benefit of the people of that town. And there is a novelty in his words, for seemingly why should there be an obligation to set up a gemaḥ, when the mitzva is that each person lend according to his ability? But there is a strong reason for this: since the mitzva of lending is incumbent on every Jew, but at the same time one person generally does not have the ability to help his fellow according to his need, therefore people must organise together as a group in order to set up a large fund that can give real help to everyone from that place who needs it. And of course in our large cities one gemaḥ fund is not enough; rather, it is a mitzva to set up a gemaḥ in each and every neighbourhood.
